title: Comparative Advantage
description: Ricardo's insight — why even worse-at-everything countries gain from trade

concepts.title: Absolute vs Comparative Advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
Absolute advantage: producing more of something with the same resources than another country can. In Ricardo's example, Portugal has absolute advantage over England in both wine and cloth.

Comparative advantage: producing something at lower opportunity cost than another country.

Ricardo's brilliant insight in 1817: trade benefits both parties even when one has absolute advantage in everything. What matters is comparative, not absolute, advantage.

Why? Because every hour spent producing X is an hour not spent producing Y. Even a country that's more productive at both should specialize in the one where its advantage is relatively larger.

concepts.title: Ricardo's Numerical Example
concepts.contentHtml:
Ricardo's classic case: England and Portugal making cloth and wine.

Suppose Portugal needs 80 hours per unit of wine and 90 hours per unit of cloth. England needs 120 for wine and 100 for cloth. Portugal is more productive at both.

But the ratios matter. Portugal gives up 90/80 = 1.125 wine for one cloth. England gives up 100/120 = 0.83 wine for one cloth. Cloth is cheaper in England (in wine terms) than in Portugal.

If England makes only cloth and Portugal only wine, then trades, both end up with more of both. The math works out as long as the trade ratio falls between each country's domestic ratio.

This isn't magic — it's reorganization. Total output rises because each country specializes where its opportunity cost is lowest.

concepts.title: Sources of Comparative Advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
Where does comparative advantage come from? Several theories.

Ricardian (technology): different countries have different productivities. Underlying differences in technology, climate, institutions.

Heckscher-Ohlin (factor endowments): countries export goods that intensively use their abundant factor. Capital-rich countries export capital-intensive goods; labor-rich countries export labor-intensive ones.

New trade theory (Krugman): increasing returns to scale and product differentiation. Countries trade similar goods (Germans and Japanese both make cars, then trade them) due to economies of scale and consumer preference for variety.

New new trade theory (Melitz): heterogeneity within industries. Only the most productive firms export; trade reorganizes within sectors as well as across them.

All these forces operate simultaneously. Modern trade economics treats them as complementary, not rival.

concepts.title: Distributional Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical theory says trade makes countries richer in aggregate. It doesn't say it makes everyone richer.

The Stolper-Samuelson theorem: trade raises returns to a country's abundant factor and lowers returns to its scarce factor. In labor-abundant countries, wages rise (trade benefits workers). In capital-abundant countries, returns to capital rise; wages of workers competing with imports may fall.

For developed economies, this implies trade tends to widen inequality between high- and low-skilled workers. The 'China shock' (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) documented exactly this: US manufacturing regions exposed to Chinese imports saw persistent declines in employment and wages.

Trade is welfare-improving in aggregate, but the gains and losses are unevenly distributed. Whether the winners compensate the losers determines whether trade is politically sustainable. Failures of compensation (in the US, weak adjustment assistance) helped fuel the trade backlash of the 2010s.

concepts.title: Limits and Critiques
concepts.contentHtml:
Comparative advantage is one of economics' most powerful insights, but it has limits.

Static analysis: Ricardo's framework treats productivities as given. Real economies grow and change. Specializing in low-productivity sectors today may foreclose high-productivity sectors tomorrow. Infant industry arguments emphasize this.

Adjustment costs: reallocating workers from declining to expanding sectors is slow and painful. The aggregate gains may take decades to materialize while the losses are immediate.

Strategic considerations: trade in critical goods (semiconductors, food, energy) raises national security questions that pure comparative advantage doesn't address.

Manipulated comparative advantage: if one country subsidizes industries to capture them artificially, the resulting trade pattern may not reflect genuine comparative advantage. The China-state-capitalism critique runs along these lines.

The classical case for trade survives all these critiques but is rarely deployed unconditionally. Modern trade policy is comparative advantage plus distributional, strategic, and dynamic considerations.

title: Trade Policy & Tariffs
description: Tariffs, quotas, NTBs, dumping, the political economy of protectionism

concepts.title: Tariffs
concepts.contentHtml:
A tariff is a tax on imports. Specific tariffs are dollar amounts per unit; ad valorem tariffs are percentages of value.

Effects of a tariff: domestic price rises by (roughly) the tariff amount. Domestic producers gain (higher prices, more output). Domestic consumers lose (higher prices, less consumption). Government collects revenue.

Net effect: deadweight loss. The losses to consumers exceed the gains to producers and government revenue, in classical analysis. The exception: a 'large country' that can move world prices may extract some of the loss from foreign producers (the 'optimal tariff'), though this triggers retaliation in practice.

Empirically, tariff incidence — who pays — is debated. The 2018-19 US tariffs on Chinese goods passed through almost completely to US consumers (Amiti, Redding, Weinstein) — the burden fell on American buyers, not Chinese sellers.

concepts.title: Quotas and Voluntary Restraints
concepts.contentHtml:
A quota caps the quantity of imports. A voluntary export restraint (VER) is a quantity limit imposed by the exporting country (typically under threat).

Both raise domestic prices similar to a tariff, but the rents flow differently. With a tariff, the government collects revenue. With a quota, the importer or exporter (depending on allocation) earns rents from the artificial scarcity.

The 1981-94 US-Japan auto VER is a famous case. Toyota and Honda 'voluntarily' limited US sales. They got higher per-unit margins (rents) on the cars they did sell; US consumers paid more; US automakers got temporary breathing space (which they largely failed to use productively).

Quotas are generally less efficient than tariffs because they raise prices without raising government revenue. Most international trade rules now restrict them, encouraging tariffs as the policy tool of choice when protection is desired.

concepts.title: Non-Tariff Barriers
concepts.contentHtml:
The most important trade barriers today aren't tariffs. They're non-tariff barriers (NTBs).

Examples: product standards (EU rules on chlorine-washed chicken), sanitary/phytosanitary measures (Japanese restrictions on certain agricultural products), licensing requirements, customs delays, government procurement preferences, technical standards, environmental rules.

NTBs are harder to measure than tariffs and harder to discipline through trade agreements. They blur the line between legitimate domestic regulation and disguised protectionism.

Modern trade agreements (CPTPP, USMCA, EU FTAs) increasingly focus on harmonizing standards and constraining NTBs. The WTO's Technical Barriers to Trade and SPS agreements try to police the line between legitimate regulation and protectionism — imperfectly.

concepts.title: Dumping & Anti-Dumping
concepts.contentHtml:
Dumping means selling exports below 'normal value' — either below cost, or below domestic prices in the exporter's home market.

WTO rules permit countries to impose anti-dumping duties when dumping causes 'material injury' to domestic industry. In practice, anti-dumping is the most-used trade protection tool, with thousands of cases globally.

Economists are mostly skeptical. Most anti-dumping cases involve normal competitive behavior (low prices in fast-changing markets, exchange rate moves, marginal cost pricing) rather than predatory dumping. Anti-dumping has become a backdoor for protectionism dressed up in legal language.

The largest anti-dumping users: the US, EU, India, and increasingly China. Targets: often China, but increasingly other emerging exporters. Steel and chemicals are perpetual hotspots.

concepts.title: Why Countries Protect Despite the Costs
concepts.contentHtml:
If trade is welfare-improving in aggregate, why is protectionism politically attractive?

Concentrated benefits, diffuse costs: tariffs help specific industries (steel, autos, textiles) visibly. They hurt millions of consumers a small amount each. Concentrated winners lobby; diffuse losers don't organize.

Distributional consequences: trade hurts specific workers and communities. Adjustment is slow and painful, even if aggregate effects are positive.

National security: some industries (defense, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, food) raise security concerns that pure-economic analysis misses.

Strategic trade: if some industries have increasing returns or strategic spillovers, capturing them ahead of rivals may pay off — though this is hard to do well in practice.

Reciprocity politics: trade openness is often negotiated; unilateral concessions weaken bargaining position.

The political economy of trade is therefore much messier than the textbook model. The default lesson — that tariffs are usually self-harming — is right, but the exceptions and the political logic explain why protectionism keeps reappearing despite the lesson.

title: Exchange Rates
description: Spot, forward, real vs nominal — purchasing power parity, interest rate parity

concepts.title: What an Exchange Rate Is
concepts.contentHtml:
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. EUR/USD = 1.10 means 1 euro buys $1.10 (or equivalently, $1 buys 0.91 euros).

Conventions vary. Some quote 'how many domestic per foreign' (Japan: 150 JPY per USD). Others quote 'how many foreign per domestic' (UK: $1.25 per GBP). Direction matters: an exchange rate 'rising' could mean appreciation or depreciation depending on the convention.

The spot rate is for immediate exchange. The forward rate is for delivery on a future date. Most currencies have liquid markets at horizons up to a year, with longer-dated forwards possible but less liquid.

concepts.title: Real vs Nominal
concepts.contentHtml:
The nominal exchange rate is what you see on screen — the price relationship between currency units.

The real exchange rate adjusts for relative price levels. RER = e × P*/P, where e is the nominal rate, P* is foreign prices, P is domestic.

The real rate measures the relative cost of foreign vs domestic goods. A depreciating real rate means your country's goods are getting cheaper relative to foreign goods — boosting exports and making imports more expensive.

For trade-balance and competitiveness analysis, real rates matter, not nominal. A country with high inflation and a stable nominal rate is actually getting expensive in real terms.

concepts.title: Purchasing Power Parity
concepts.contentHtml:
PPP says that, in the long run, a basket of goods should cost the same when valued in a common currency. If a Big Mac costs $5 in the US and ¥600 in Japan, the implied PPP rate is 120 yen/$. If the actual rate is 150, the yen is undervalued by PPP (Japanese goods are 'cheap' in dollar terms).

The Economist's Big Mac Index publicizes this comparison annually. More rigorous PPP indices use broader baskets — the World Bank's International Comparison Program.

PPP holds approximately for traded goods over very long horizons (decades), but exchange rates can deviate from PPP for years. Reasons: non-tradeables (haircuts, real estate), tariffs and trade frictions, productivity differences, capital flows.

For comparing living standards across countries, PPP-adjusted income is the right concept. China's GDP at market exchange rates is about two-thirds of US GDP; at PPP, it's about 130%.

concepts.title: Interest Rate Parity
concepts.contentHtml:
Interest rate parity says: forward exchange rates compensate for interest rate differentials.

If US rates are 5% and Japanese rates are 1%, an investor borrowing yen and lending dollars seems to earn the difference. But by no-arbitrage, the forward yen/dollar rate must build in a forward discount on the dollar that exactly offsets the interest gain once the currency risk is hedged.

The covered version (CIP): F/S = (1+i)/(1+i*). Before 2008 this held tightly in liquid markets, since deviations would be arbitrage opportunities; since then small but persistent deviations have appeared as bank balance-sheet costs limit arbitrage (Du, Tarlow and Verdelhan).

The uncovered version (UIP) — that the spot rate change equals the interest differential — fails empirically. The 'forward premium puzzle': high-interest currencies tend to appreciate on average, the opposite of what UIP predicts. This is the basis of the carry trade.

The CIP/UIP gap is one of finance's most studied puzzles. Most explanations involve risk premia, expectational errors, or peso problems.

concepts.title: What Drives Exchange Rates
concepts.contentHtml:
Exchange rates over short horizons are notoriously hard to predict. Famous Meese-Rogoff (1983) result: exchange-rate models couldn't beat a random walk in out-of-sample forecasting at horizons of one to twelve months.

Over longer horizons, fundamentals do matter. Persistent factors:

Trade balances: persistent surpluses tend to support currency value over time, deficits the reverse.

Interest rate differentials: attract or repel capital flows.

Productivity differentials: Balassa-Samuelson — fast-productivity-growth countries have appreciating real currencies.

Risk sentiment: 'safe haven' currencies (USD, JPY, CHF) appreciate in crises; 'risky' EM currencies depreciate.

Carry-trade flows: high-yielders attract speculative inflows during calm periods, suffer reversals in panic.

The mix of fundamentals and sentiment makes exchange rates one of the most volatile, and least predictable, asset prices in finance.

title: Balance of Payments
description: Current account, capital account, why they always balance, twin deficits

concepts.title: What the Balance of Payments Records
concepts.contentHtml:
The balance of payments (BoP) is a comprehensive accounting of all transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period.

Two main accounts.

Current account: goods and services trade, factor income (interest, dividends, wages from abroad), and unilateral transfers (remittances, aid). Captures real-economy flows.

Financial account (also called capital account, with some terminology variation): purchases and sales of financial assets — FDI, portfolio flows, central bank reserves.

By accounting identity, the two must sum to zero (with a 'errors and omissions' fudge factor in practice). Every payment in must be a payment out somewhere.

concepts.title: Why Current = Negative Capital
concepts.contentHtml:
If a country runs a current account deficit (importing more than exporting, net), where does the money to pay for those imports come from?

Foreigners. Either they're lending the country money (buying its bonds, parking deposits) or buying its assets (FDI, equities, real estate). That's a positive capital account.

Symmetrically, current account surpluses (exporting more than importing) imply lending to or investing in foreign countries — negative capital account.

This is identity, not theory. It must hold. The interesting question is which side drives which: do trade flows drive financing flows, or does desire to hold foreign assets drive trade flows? In modern integrated capital markets, the latter often dominates — financial flows are huge multiples of trade flows.

concepts.title: Persistent Imbalances
concepts.contentHtml:
Some countries run persistent current account deficits (US, UK, Australia). Others run persistent surpluses (Germany, China for decades, Japan, Saudi Arabia).

The US has run current account deficits almost every year since 1982. By 2024, accumulated foreign claims on the US (Net International Investment Position) were around -$26 trillion at end-2024: the world holds enormous amounts of US assets, including stocks, corporate bonds and Treasuries.

Are persistent deficits dangerous? Conventional wisdom said yes — eventually rebalancing would force a sharp correction. But for the US, the dollar's reserve currency status has allowed deficits to persist far longer than 'sustainability' analyses predicted.

For non-reserve countries, persistent deficits are riskier. They eventually require either painful adjustment (currency depreciation, recession) or external rescue (IMF programs).

concepts.title: Twin Deficits
concepts.contentHtml:
The twin deficits hypothesis: budget deficits and current account deficits move together.

Logic: a national savings identity. (S − I) = (X − M) + (G − T). Private savings minus investment equals net exports plus the government deficit. If government runs a deficit, something else must give — either private savings rises, or current account weakens.

The 1980s US Reagan-era experience matched the theory: Reagan's deficits coincided with widening US trade deficits. The mechanism: deficits raised real rates, attracted capital inflows, strengthened the dollar, hurt exports.

The relationship is real but not mechanical. Many other factors affect both. The 1990s saw US fiscal surpluses but persistent trade deficits. The 2008-09 crisis saw both deficits widen for distinct reasons.

The hypothesis is a useful tendency, not an inviolable law.

concepts.title: Crisis Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Current account imbalances can be sustainable for long periods, then unwind violently.

Pattern: a country runs persistent current account deficits financed by foreign borrowing. Foreign creditors are happy as long as growth is strong and currency is stable. Then something triggers a reassessment — political risk, commodity shock, banking problem. Capital flows reverse suddenly.

The currency collapses. Foreign-currency debt becomes unaffordable. Banks fail. Recession follows.

This is the sudden stop pattern that hit Mexico (1994), East Asia (1997), Russia (1998), Argentina (2001), Iceland (2008), Greece (2010), and many others. Common features: large current account deficits, foreign-currency borrowing, fixed exchange rate or weak floating arrangement, weak banking supervision.

Modern early-warning indicators watch current account deficits as % of GDP, foreign-currency debt levels, and reserves coverage. Above certain thresholds (e.g., current account deficit > 4-5% of GDP for several years), risk rises sharply.

title: Currency Unions & Crises
description: Optimal currency areas, the Euro, sudden stops, the trilemma

concepts.title: Optimal Currency Areas
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Mundell's 1961 framework asks: when does it make sense for multiple countries to share a currency?

Benefits of shared currency: eliminates exchange-rate risk, lowers transaction costs, increases trade and investment within the union, may impart inflation discipline.

Costs: loss of independent monetary policy, loss of exchange-rate adjustment as a shock absorber.

The currency union is optimal when:

1. Countries face similar shocks (so common monetary policy fits all).

2. Labor and capital move freely (workers can migrate when shocks differ).

3. Wages and prices are flexible.

4. There are fiscal transfers across regions to absorb asymmetric shocks.

The US satisfies these conditions reasonably well. The eurozone, less so.

concepts.title: The Euro
concepts.contentHtml:
The euro launched in 1999 as accounting currency, in 2002 as physical currency. It now covers 21 EU member states (Bulgaria joined in 2026) with ~350 million people.

The political project: deepen European integration, prevent currency crises within Europe (such as those of the early 1990s), increase Europe's monetary weight globally.

The economic reality: the eurozone is suboptimal as a currency area by Mundell's criteria. Labor mobility is limited (language, culture). Wages are sticky. Fiscal transfers are minimal — the EU budget is ~1% of GDP, vs ~20% for US federal spending. Different countries face different shocks (Germany's industrial economy ≠ Greece's tourism economy).

The euro project worked through the early 2000s as capital flowed from north to south, financing Mediterranean growth. It came undone in 2010-12 when those flows reversed.

concepts.title: The Eurozone Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
2010-12 brought the eurozone's deepest test. Trigger: Greek revelations of much larger budget deficits than reported. Bond yields spiked.

The crisis spread to Ireland (banking crisis), Portugal, Spain, Italy. Investors began doubting that the euro itself was sustainable. Country-level bond yields diverged dramatically.

Standard responses (currency devaluation, monetary easing for the affected country) were unavailable. Each country was stuck with euro membership but couldn't run national monetary policy.

Resolution came piecemeal: ECB liquidity support, EFSF/ESM bailout funds, Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' commitment in July 2012, and severe austerity programs in periphery countries. The euro survived, but at substantial cost in unemployment (Spain and Greece saw youth unemployment pass 50% and overall unemployment reach 25%+) and political instability.

concepts.title: Sudden Stops & Asymmetric Adjustment
concepts.contentHtml:
The eurozone crisis illustrated a sudden stop phenomenon within a currency union.

Pre-crisis, German savings flowed to Spain, Greece, Portugal — funding construction booms and current account deficits. Post-crisis, those flows reversed abruptly. But unlike a normal sudden stop, the affected countries couldn't depreciate their currency.

Adjustment had to come through 'internal devaluation' — falling nominal wages and prices to restore competitiveness. This is far slower and more painful than exchange-rate adjustment. Greece's nominal GDP fell roughly 25% from 2008 to 2016.

Asymmetric adjustment is a deep flaw of incomplete currency unions. The deficit country has to bear the brunt; the surplus country is under no symmetric pressure to inflate. This was the German Mark experience writ large for the entire south.

concepts.title: Lessons for Currency Unions
concepts.contentHtml:
The eurozone crisis catalyzed major institutional reforms.

Banking union: common supervision (Single Supervisory Mechanism), common resolution (Single Resolution Mechanism), common deposit insurance (still incomplete).

European Stability Mechanism: permanent bailout fund.

OMT: ECB power to buy bonds of stressed sovereigns.

Fiscal discipline: tighter rules on deficits and debt (though enforcement remains weak).

What's still missing: substantial automatic fiscal transfers across countries, full deposit insurance, eurobonds. The euro remains a currency without a complete fiscal-political backing — partly stable, partly fragile.

For other currency unions, existing or proposed (the CFA franc zones in West and Central Africa, Gulf Cooperation Council talks of a Gulf currency, Latin American proposals), the eurozone is both inspiration and cautionary tale. Currency union without political union is doable but expensive when it goes wrong.

title: Capital Flows: Inflows & Outflows
description: FDI vs portfolio vs hot money, sudden stops, capital controls, the global savings glut

concepts.title: Types of Capital Flows
concepts.contentHtml:
Not all capital flows are alike. They differ in stability, productivity contribution, and risk profile.

Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): long-term ownership stakes in productive assets — factories, subsidiaries. Most stable. Brings management, technology, market access.

Portfolio investment: stocks and bonds purchased without management control. More liquid, more volatile.

Bank lending: loans across borders, including interbank funding. Can be very stable or very flighty depending on conditions.

Other: trade credit, derivatives, remittances.

The general principle: longer-duration, equity-style flows are more stable; shorter-duration, debt-style flows are more flighty. The 1997 Asian crisis and 2008 European crisis both featured sudden reversals of bank lending.

concepts.title: Hot Money
concepts.contentHtml:
Hot money refers to short-term capital flows that chase returns and exit at any sign of trouble. Mostly bank lending, money-market funds, and carry-trade flows.

The phenomenon: when emerging-market interest rates exceed developed-market rates, investors borrow cheaply abroad and lend at higher EM rates. As long as exchange rates are stable, this is profitable.

The risk: at any sign of EM trouble — political upheaval, commodity shock, US rate increases — these flows reverse. Rapid outflows depress the currency, raise local rates, deepen the crisis.

The 2013 'taper tantrum' (when the Fed signaled quantitative easing would end) hit emerging markets hard precisely because hot money had built up during the QE years.

Hot money exemplifies the curse of liquid capital markets for small economies: useful capital while it's flowing in, devastating when it flees.

concepts.title: Sudden Stops
concepts.contentHtml:
A sudden stop is an abrupt reversal of capital inflows. Calvo's 1998 paper popularized the term; the phenomenon recurs across emerging markets.

Pattern:

1. Country attracts capital inflows during expansion. Currency appreciates, current account deficit widens.

2. Trigger arrives: external shock, political event, contagion from another country.

3. Capital flees. Currency collapses. Foreign-currency debt becomes unaffordable.

4. Banking crisis. Investment collapses. Recession.

5. Adjustment via deep recession, often IMF program.

Famous cases: Mexico 1994, East Asia 1997, Russia 1998, Argentina 2001, Iceland 2008, Greece 2010, Turkey 2018, Sri Lanka 2022, Argentina (again) 2018.

Common ingredients: large capital inflows, foreign-currency borrowing, fixed or quasi-fixed exchange rate, weak banking supervision. Countries with floating rates and reserves tend to weather sudden stops better but not avoid them entirely.

concepts.title: Capital Controls
concepts.contentHtml:
Capital controls are restrictions on cross-border financial flows. Inflow controls (taxes, reserve requirements on foreign borrowing) try to slow hot money. Outflow controls (limits on residents moving money abroad) try to prevent capital flight during stress.

The 1990s consensus was that capital controls were always bad — interfering with efficient global allocation. Most emerging markets liberalized.

The 2010s consensus shifted. The IMF officially endorsed targeted, temporary capital controls in 2012 — a major reversal. Macroprudential measures (loan-to-value caps, debt-to-income limits, foreign-currency lending restrictions) gained acceptance.

Empirically, well-designed inflow controls (Chile's 1990s unremunerated reserve requirement, Brazil's IOF tax) reduce financial fragility without crippling growth. Outflow controls in crises (Malaysia 1998, Iceland 2008, Greece 2015) can buy time for adjustment but distort markets and risk capital flight when lifted.

The instrument is no longer taboo, but how to use it well remains contested.

concepts.title: The Global Savings Glut
concepts.contentHtml:
Ben Bernanke's 2005 hypothesis: the world has too much savings chasing too few investment opportunities. The result: low global real interest rates and large capital flows from surplus countries (China, Germany, Saudi Arabia, Japan) to deficit countries (US, UK, Spain).

Why? Aging populations save more. Emerging markets self-insure with reserves after the 1997 crisis. Inequality concentrates wealth in high-savings hands. Productive investment opportunities have shrunk relative to capital available.

Implications: low real rates worldwide. Asset price inflation as savings chase returns. Bubble vulnerability — pre-2008 housing bubbles were partly financed by surplus-country savings.

The savings glut hypothesis became more controversial post-2020 as inflation surged. Some interpret the inflation spike as the glut ending; others as a temporary disruption that will reverse. The longer-term path of global real rates remains one of macro's most consequential open questions, with profound implications for growth, asset prices, and fiscal policy.
